caps.en:
Major accidents may or may not have associated deaths. Two people
died in this head-on collision.

A head-on collision. Expect injuries to the occupant's right side, as if
he/she traveled toward the point of impact

This truck ran into a bridge. Miraculously, the driver walked away
from the accident. Unfortunately, his brother, who was in the cab's sleeping
compartment, died.
The car came to rest against a pole. The passenger may have "intrusion" injuries from the impacted door

The driver of this vehicle was caught upside down in his seatbelt and
suffocated [postural asphyxiation).
The examiner or investigator should know the position of the decedent in the vehicle

This driver was pinned in the wreckage, and sustained impressive
head trauma
This driver died of a combination of head and chest trauma.

This occupant had an open skull fracture. Portions of her skull are
next to her shoulder
Broken windshield resulting from the impact of the passenger's head.

Emergency personnel are among the first to arrive at the accident
scene. They are good sources of information concerning the location of the
body/lsodies and whether the victims were dead or alive when first viewed

A van T-boned a smaller vehicle, after which both were damaged by
fire. The occupants were also thermally injured.

A burned body in the car after the accident and subsequent fire. An
autopsy would prove if the person died from the fire or the impact, or a combination of the two

A close-up of a thermally injured occupant. Most bodies are burned
after death. Testing for carbon monoxide in the blood and an examination for
soot in the airway will prove if the person was alive or dead at the time of the fire

Papers and a watch at the scene helped to identify the burned remains
of the driver

This woman was lying outside the car. Was she in this position
when first discovered? The investigator must speak with the first people to arrive
at the scene.

One of the occupants of the accident vehicle was thrown out of the
car. It is important to decide if he was driving

Careful examination of the vehicle may reveal areas on or in the car
where the occupant made contact. There is brain material in this door frame.

The damage to this boat occurred after it became unhitched while
being towed. It traveled across the median and struck a Vollzswagen head-on,
killing the driver of the car

The driver of this vehicle was intoxicated, missed a turn, and drove
into the pond. He drowned. There were no bodily injuries.

This truck traveled under a parked tractor trailer, decapitating the
driver. The point of impact of the driver's head on the truck was apparent

The grass and weeds stuck in this grill indicate of how the truck
rolled after the accident.

Skid marks are helpful when determining whether or not a death
was an accident or suicide
Faint tire marks on the sidewallz. This finding helped in reconstructing a hit-and-run homicide.
Scrape marks of the vehicle on the median concrete divider
Impact site on the concrete from the driver's head.

Motorcyclists are sometimes told to aim for an animal in the road.
If they do, chances are they will miss the animal. Unfortunately, that did not
work this time. The motorcyclist died after hitting the deer at an estimated speed
of 70 mph. He died of head trauma; he was wearing a helmet

This vehicle traveled straight into a tree. This was a suicide. The
driver also had incised wounds on one of his wrists.

The driver of this car drove her vehicle into a rock wall. See next
photo

The stuck speedometer indicates how fast the car was traveling
when it hit the wall. See next photo.
A suicide note was discovered in the trunk

Leather sole shoes may have impressions from the brake or accelerator pedals. This may give a clue as to how the driver was reacting at the time
of the accident.

Pedal marks on the sole. These are not distinct enough to distinguish
between the brake and accelerator pedals

The initial site of a high-speed impact. The distance from the impact
site to the body's location gives an indication of the vehicle's speed at the moment
of impact. See next photo.
The body came to rest yards away from the impact site

Pedestrians may be struck multiple times, especially on highways.
Initial impact sites may be difficult to evaluate.
Extremities may be torn off in high-speed pedestrian accidents

This person was crushed from being run over. Such extensive injuries
make it difficult to identify impact sites.

The heights of fractures must be measured. The fracture heights
may be matched to bumper heights. The distances may indicate whether or not
the vehicle was braking at the time of impact. See next photo

This is the vehicle that struck the man in the previous photo. The
bumper height can be matched to the height of the fractures.

Fractured bones may not match the external sites of impact. The
impact site in the thigh area is quite far from the end of the fracture. The impact
site is more important than the location of the end of the fracture

The open fracture of this lower leg occurred when the pedestrian
was struck; at the time, this leg was in contact with the ground.

Multiple points of impact from being struck during a hit-and-run.
There are pattern injuries that can be matched to the vehicle

Pedestrian. Extensive injuries of the legs and pelvis from the initial
impact.

Patterns from the vehicle may be present. The arrows outline a
headlight on this man's leg

Damaged areas on a vehicle may need to be examined because the
area may be matched to injuries on the body.

This pedestrian was struck by a truck. Paint chips on the clothing
and this mark with the pale center on his leg helped to identify the particular
type of truck
Pieces of the vehicle may be embedded in the body.

Pedestrian. Clothing may be disoriented and pulled off. Some people
may be "knocked out" of their shoes

Sharply defined tire markings on the chest and abdomen. These
marks can be matched to the tire that caused the injury.
Tire mark on the right arm
Another tire pattern on an arm.

The tread pattern on the child's head may be matched to the vehicle
that struck him
These marks were caused by a tire stretching the skin.
More stretch marks from a tire
Pedestrian. Pattern paint mark from the vehicle

Adult pedestrians tend to be "run under" when struck by automobiles. This man was struck and lifted into the air, and came to rest on the car's
top and windshield. See next photo.
A closer view of the body's final resting position

Pedestrians may receive injuries from striking the vehicle after being
thrown into the air. There may also be secondary impact sites on the vehicles.

The girl wearing this bracelet was struck with such force that the
pendant abraded the skin. See next photo

The force of the impact was so great that the vertebral column was
completely torn away from the base of the skull. No spinal cord is visible in the
foramen where it is normally located (arrow)
Pedestrian. X-ray of fractured leg at the impact site
Impact lacerations and abrasions from the roadway.
Pebble abrasions from the roadway

Road rash of the face. The rougher the roadway surfaces, the deeper
and more impressive the injuries.
Stretch marks from being struck on the side

Lacerations of the scrotum with evisceration of the testicle. There
was no direct impact to the scrotum. The pressure from the force of the impact
caused the skin rupture.
This scalp with ear was discovered on the truck involved in a hitand-run

This boy was decapitated after a hit-and-run. The distance of the
head from the body helped determine the speed of the car.
The boy's head was reattached and there was an open casket funeral

Retroperitoneal hemorrhage. This state trooper was struck by a
drunk driver's car while issuing a ticket to another drunk driver.

Pieces of paint and other material found on clothing are important
to collect. They may be matched to missing areas on a vehicle, as in this case

Glass fragments caused these irregularly shaped abrasions of the
chest.

The angulated cuts on this man's face were caused by contact with
the side window. The tempered glass making up the side window fractured in
cubes. These injuries are called "dicing abrasions," or "glass dicing."

The black eyes (spectacle hemorrhages) were caused by blood seeping
down into the face from fractures of the skull above the eyes.
Pattern marks on a child's face from an impact with the dashboard
Pattern mark on the left side of the face caused by a pole.
Dicing abrasions on the face of a passenger

This man's forehead is abraded and torn from an impact with the
windshield
Woman struck by a pole while a passenger in a car
Woman hit by the edge of a sign while seated in a car

An impact under the chin caused hyperextension injuries to the
spinal cord and brain

Transection of the brainstem between the medulla and pons (arrow).
This type of injury occurs in a violent hyperextension of the head

Extensive soft tissue hemorrhage in the back of the neck from a
severe whiplash or hyperextension injury

X-ray of the neck revealing a subluxation [slippage] of the vertebral
column. This type of injury causes sudden death by impingement of the spinal
cord. Actual fractures of the cervical vertebral column are not as common as
thought
Child with burn marks on the face.
The driver died after ejection when his head hit the tree

Laceration in the web of the hand. This indicated the driver was
holding the steering wheel during impact.

Air bags may prevent external injuries. This woman died from a
ruptured aorta after the accident. She had no external injuries

This is the type of external injury typically resulted from impacting
the steering column in head-on collisions, and was common prior to the use of
seat belts and air bags.
Pattern seatbelt marks on the shoulder and chest of a passenger
Seatbelt marks on a driver

These photos of a vehicle occupant reveal injuries to the shoulder
and upper arm. The arrow points to the mark made by a seat belt, which proves
the decedent was the driver
Abrasions from a seat [lap)belt.
Slight abrasions of the chest from the seatbelt
Seatbelt mark on the shoulder.
The pattern of the clothing can be seen on the skin
The abraded areas were caused by the decedent's clothing.

The only mark on this man's body was this contusion from a truck's
cab. He was trapped after he attempted to jump clear of the truck as it began to
roll over. He died of asphyxiation

The driver was ejected and pinned after the truck overturned. There
were numerous petechiae and prominent congestion of the face from
compression.
Congestion of the face from compression asphyxia

In this accident, the car overturned and one of the passengers was
discovered dead, lying in this position. See next photo.
A closer view reveals the boy's head (arrow) to be tightly compressed against his chest. He died from positional asphyxiation
Pressure marks across the uper chest from compression.

This driver had a fracture of the leg and many other nonspecific
injuries

This is an example of "road rash" after the man was ejected from
the vehicle and slid across the road.
Impaled during ejection
Impaled with a pole
This boy was impaled after ejection.
Linear abrasions from the roadway
Burn marks of the chest as the result of an ejection and rollover.

Burns on the hip and buttoclzs from a muffler, which occurred
during a rollover

This open fracture of the forearm occurred while the driver grabbed
the steering wheel.
Closed fractures of the ankles

Lower leg and ankle fractures after the legs and feet were caught
under the seat during a head-on collision.

Open fracture of the ankle occurred after the foot was caught under
the seat

Fracture of the femur at the scene. This scene photo leaves little
doubt as to the cause of the fracture.

This is not an injury from the steering wheel. It is an abrasion that
resulted from shocking the decedent during CPR. Note similar marks on the left
side of the chest

Occupants may sustain many different kinds of injuries. This man
had some pattern marks on the abdomen that were matched to part of the seat
in the car.

Extensive lacerations of the liver from an impact with the abdomen
and lower chest
Laceration of the heart after a head-on collision.

This heart was completely torn off and discovered floating in the
left chest cavity after a head-on collision

This sutured laceration in the aorta of a driver is in the area
commonly torn during a frontal or side impact.

This is an unusual tear in the aorta. The tear is usually horizontal
and not vertical
Laceration of the aorta after a head-on collision.

There may be multiple rib fractures and soft tissue bleeding in any
impact to the chest

A child with a collapsed right lung. Note how far the lung has
collapsed away from the chest wall. This is an indication there was a build-up
of air in the chest cavity.

A cutting injury of the neck that occurred during an accident. It
loolzs as if a knife caused the injury

Hemorrhage in the soft tissue behind the ear (Battle's sign) is an
indication of a sltull fracture.

Extensive superficial abrasions of the face caused by being thrown
around the inside of a tractor. See next photo

Extensive subscalpular hemorrhage from the multiple impacts.
There was no trauma to the brain.

Fractures of the skull in the areas indicated by arrows will cause
bleeding in the ear canals. There may be an associated bluish discoloration of
the skin behind the ears (Battle's sign)

A hinged fracture of the slzull. External examination would indicate
blood in the decedent's ear canals.

Not all victims die right away. This person has multiple pressure
sores (decubitus ulcers) and died from infection long after the accident. The death
is still considered a complication of the accident

This accident did not appear serious; however, the driver was dead.
See next photo.

There was no damage to the vehicle or apparent injury to the driver.
Autopsy revealed the driver died of a heart attack. When an accident is minor
and the driver is dead, the investigator must first consider a natural cause
This was the scene of a head-on collision. See next photo.

The driver's wife, seated on the passenger side, had a broken arm
only. See next photo

The driver was caught in the cab. The extrication took over an
hour and the man survived for only a short time in the emergency room.
Knowledge of the scene is important for understanding the cause of death.

A car left the right side of the roadway at this curve. The highway
patrol estimated the car's speed at 40 to 45 mph when it left the road. See next
photo

The car came to rest in the adjacent field and the driver was dead
in the front seat. The arrow points to a ruler, which measures the size of the
open window. The driver's hat was discovered next to a fence at the point of
initial impact. See next photo.

The driver was discovered with his head below the passenger's seat.
This was the only area of blood in the car. See next photo

The driver had multiple skull fractures and an open laceration of
the scalp from a frontal impact; however, there were no points of impact seen
inside the car. Such cases remain a mystery.

A boy was riding his bicycle home after work one night. The back
wheel of the bicycle revealed he was struck from behind. The body was not at
the scene of initial impact. See next photo

The body was discovered approximately 3 miles from the site of
the accident. The line of blood next to the body could be followed for 2.5 miles.
See next photo.

There were considerable injuries to his side from being dragged.
See next photo

There were black rubbing marks from the tires of the truck. The
only significant injuries to the body were those from being dragged. See next
photo.

There were abrasions of the face; however, there was no head
trauma. See next photo

The truclz was discovered in a trailer park. The owner was inside.
See next photo.

The truclz showed signs that the bike was struck by the front of
the truclz. See next photo

The driver's shoes were in the sink. He had attempted to wash
them. Blood on the shoes matched that of the decedent. The driver had no license
and had been convicted three times for drunk driving. He was sent to jail for 25
years.

Most motorcyclists die from head trauma even if they are wearing
helmets

The body tends to be thrown free of the motorcycle and impact
against the ground.

Some helmets, such as this one, are more protective because they
cover the entire head. However, at high rates of speed, helmets do not guard
against serious injury
This motorcyclist hit a tree head-on at 50 to 55 mph.

This 15-year-oldwas the passenger in a car that went out of control,
flipped and hit a tree. He was belted in. There were few external signs of trauma.
Notice the lap belt mark on his hip. See next photo
He also had a belt mark on his right shoulder. See next photo.

There was blood In the soft tissue high in the neck U
the skin.

A deeper cut reveals a tearing of the ligaments and a marked
displacement of the vertebral column. Subsequent examination revealed the
spinal cord had been severed. Occasionally, injuries to the neck may only be
detected by examining the back of the neck

This car skidded off the highway, traveled down an embankment
and ended up in the stream. See next photo.
The driver was not in the burned car. See next photo

The driver was discovered on the hill. Both he and the surrounding
area had been burned. Autopsy revealed no soot in the airway and no carbon
monoxide in his blood. There were no injuries to the body except for the thermal
damage. He died from being compressed as the car rolled over him
